newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean bank reserve cut to boost bourse - analysts.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean bank reserve cut to boost bourse - analysts.

text.p: A Bank of Korea official on Wednesday said reserve requirements would be cut for South Korean banks, and analysts predicted the move would result in lower interest rates and a boost to the stock market.
Reserve requirements -- the percentage of deposits that domestic banks must set aside with the central bank -- will be cut by an average of two percentage points on November 8, the official said.
Average requirements are now around 7.5 percent.
An official announcement would be made on Thursday, the official said.
"I think this news will boost tomorrow's market, especially banking stocks," said Hyundai Securities market analyst Lee Sang-koo.
The market closed on Wednesday down 7.24 points to 811.98 points in lacklustre trading before news of the cut.
Analysts said the central bank's action was mainly aimed at boosting South Korea's sagging economy.

"Public opinion is now saying that lending rates are too high and that is part of the reason that South Korean products are losing their international competitiveness," said Kim Byong-sok, a banking analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities.
Benchmark three-year corporate bond yields are currently at around 12 percent.
High interest rates are cutting into corporate profits, which are coming under increasing pressure from a decline in South Korea's exports.
The trade deficit was expected to widen to a record $19 billion this year, almost double last year's shortfall, according to the trade ministry.

The cut is seen as part of a move to gradually bring domestic interest rates in line with global rates as South Korea prepares to enter the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the analysts said.
Seoul was invited to join the Paris-based club of rich nations earlier this month.
Mok Young-chung, a banking analyst with ING Barings Securities, said South Korea's reserve requirements were now higher than the OECD average.
Japan's were one percent, Germany below two percent, and France below one percent, Mok said.
"Overall liquidity isn't expected to rise because the central bank is expected to cut its rediscount loans," Mok added.
Analysts said the reserve requirement cut was expected to have more of a psychological impact on the market.
"This will reignite the hopes of an interest rate cut which had driven the market higher recently," said Hyundai's Lee.
The stock market slumped this week on a technical consolidation after staging a sharp rally earlier this month, brokers said.
The ceiling for foreign shareholders was raised to 20 percent from the previous 18 on October 1.
